multi_hop_neighbors.edge: The fraternity may pursue legal action for defamation.
A private individual must prove that a false factual statement was published about them that harmed their reputation.
Defamation law must be balanced against freedom of speech protections.
Will Dana, the managing editor of Rolling Stone, issued an apology to readers and those affected by the flawed article.
Individual members of the fraternity may have a case for defamation if the statements are about a small group.
Other fraternities on campus may have a harder time bringing a defamation lawsuit.
Rolling Stone was reviewed by Columbia Journalism School professors.
The fraternity and UVA administrators and students were damaged by the story and its fallout.
Defamation cases are often threatened but rarely filed.
